title: The Gaon the Aderet: Rabbi of Ponevezh, Mir and Jerusalem
source_file: הגאון האדר-ת- רבה של פוניבז_, מיר וירושלים.docx
content:
The Gaon the Aderet: Rabbi of Ponevezh, Mir and Jerusalem
The text surveys the life and the great spiritual legacy of the Gaon the Aderet, who was one of the prominent luminaries of Torah in Lithuania and Jerusalem in the 19th century and at the beginning of the 20th century. The article traces the course of his life from a young prodigy to extensive communal leadership, emphasizing his extraordinary moral integrity and his choice of a life of poverty and self-sacrifice for the sake of the public. The author goes deeply into the description of his public work in Jerusalem, which included social and halakhic reforms in the areas of the eruv, the weights and charity, alongside a prolific Torah writing of more than a hundred books that combine phenomenal erudition with profound humility. Finally, the source clarifies the unique bond with his son-in-law, Rav Kook (the Ra'ayah), who saw in the figure of the Aderet a living bridge between the world of practical halakha and the spiritual world of faith, a bond immortalized in the fundamental work "Eder HaYakar."
The Work, Torah Teaching and Leadership of the Gaon the Aderet: Rabbi of Ponevezh, Mir and Jerusalem
Biography and Stations of Life: The Path of Growth of a Halakhic Giant
The Gaon Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim, known by his literary and public epithet the Aderet, was born on 6 Sivan 5603 (4 June 1843) in the town of Pikeln (Pikelin) in the Kovno district of Lithuania, which was at that time under the rule of the Russian Empire.[1] He was born to his father, the Gaon Rabbi Binyamin Rabinowitz, author of the fundamental work "Mishnat Rabbi Binyamin," who served as the local rabbi.[2] His birth took place together with the birth of his twin brother, Rabbi Zvi Yehuda, and from this derives the family dynasty's surname "Teomim" (twins).[2] Both brothers revealed themselves from a very young age as extraordinary Torah prodigies; already at the age of thirteen or fourteen the two jointly composed a comprehensive scholarly book on the rules of the Talmud called "Shevet Achim."[2, 3] At only sixteen the Aderet testified of himself that he had completed the study and memorization of all the tractates of the Babylonian Talmud with enormous speed, and that his memory had absorbed all the details and the general rules down to the finest particulars.[2, 3]
In 5621 (1861) the Aderet married the daughter of the wealthy R. Aryeh Leib Chazan of Ponevezh, and moved to live in his father-in-law's house, where he applied himself to his studies with supreme diligence in the local study hall called "the Kloyz."[2] During those years he was stricken with a severe and painful eye disease that prevented him from reading and studying regularly, and in its wake he was forced to move for a time to the house of his father, who was serving at that time as the rabbi of the town of Vilkomir.[2] The Aderet's moral sensitivity was already expressed in his youth, when he refused many rabbinic offers made to him, foremost among them the offer to serve as rabbi in his native town of Pikeln; the refusal stemmed from the fact that the town's previous rabbi, who had been stricken with severe paralysis, was still alive, and the Aderet feared that accepting the post would hurt the feelings and the public standing of the elderly rabbi.[2]
In 5632 (1872), when he was only twenty-nine years old, the Aderet was appointed to serve as the rabbi of Ponevezh – one of the important and large communities of Lithuania – in place of Rabbi Hillel Milikowsky, the foremost disciple of Rabbi Israel Salanter.[1, 3] The Aderet led the community of Ponevezh for eighteen years.[1, 2, 3] This period was characterized by extensive and extraordinary charitable activity; he cared for the needs of the poor and the needy and even traveled himself to raise donations for them.[1, 2] Nevertheless, his official rabbinic salary was meager and limited, and his family lived in conditions of shameful poverty.[1, 2, 4] Because of the poverty and the lack of elementary medical means, the Aderet experienced unbearably severe family tragedies, as seven to nine of his twelve children died of various illnesses while still young.[2, 4]
In 5646 (1886) the Aderet's daughter, Alte Batsheva, married Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaKohen Kook (the Ra'ayah).[1] The heavy poverty prevented the Aderet from meeting his dowry obligations, and he was forced to give up his own bed for the young couple.[2] Three years later Alte Batsheva died in the prime of her life.[1] Out of a strong desire to preserve the unique Torah and family bond that had been formed with Rav Kook, the Aderet proposed that he marry his orphaned niece, Reiza Rivka (the daughter of his twin brother, Rabbi Zvi Yehuda), whom the Aderet had raised in his home as a daughter.[1, 2] Rav Kook accepted the proposal, and thus the close family bond was preserved.[1, 2]
In 5653 (1893) the Aderet acceded to the request of the members of the Mir community to serve as their rabbi.[1, 2] The move to Mir, which was a smaller and poorer community than Ponevezh, stemmed mainly from his aspiration to serve in a town in which the famous Mir yeshiva operated and in which the influences of the Haskalah (Enlightenment) movement were less widespread.[2] When the leaders of Ponevezh discovered his intention to leave, they offered to double his salary, and prominent rabbis (among them the author of the "Sdei Chemed") ruled for him that he was halakhically permitted to retract his commitment to Mir.[2] The Aderet was inclined to remain in Ponevezh because of his family's difficulties, but his final decision to move took shape when he learned of a local craftsman who had cancelled a contract with his worker with a socially destructive argument: "If the rabbi is permitted to cancel a commitment, so am I."[2] The Aderet's understanding that the personal example of the leader stands above any formal halakhic permission led him to keep his word and move to Mir in order to prevent a desecration of God's name and moral laxity among the public.[2, 4]
In 5661 (1901), following the recommendation of Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski and the invitation of the elderly rabbi of Jerusalem, Rabbi Shmuel Salant, the Aderet immigrated to the Land of Israel to serve as his assistant and his future successor in the leadership of the Ashkenazi community in Jerusalem.[2, 3] Despite a certain chronological confusion found in some of the later sources, which give the year of his immigration as 5666 (1906), the immigration in fact took place on 26 Adar 5661 (1901), and the Aderet served in Jerusalem until his passing in the year 5665.[1, 2, 3] Upon his arrival in Jerusalem, the elderly Rabbi Shmuel Salant awaited him near the Shaare Zedek hospital and announced the transfer of the crown of the rabbinate to him.[2, 3] Out of extraordinary humility, the Aderet refused to sit on Rabbi Salant's official chair and insisted on sitting only beside him.[2, 3]
His Public Work and Religious Reforms in Jerusalem
The arrival of the Aderet in Jerusalem breathed a new spirit of life into the public and religious institutions of the Old Yishuv.[2, 5] The courtyard of the Old Yishuv in the Old City was a focus of traditional and simple Jewish life, saturated with difficulties of livelihood and internal tensions.[5] Immediately upon his arrival the Aderet identified the need to strengthen the halakhic and social infrastructure of the city, and took a series of practical and corrective steps:
The repair of the city eruv was one of the Aderet's central and most complex initiatives in Jerusalem.[1, 2] He initiated and established a comprehensive halakhic eruv that connected the Old City with the new neighborhoods that had begun to develop outside the walls.[1, 2] Because of principled halakhic and political objections on the part of certain zealous elements in the city, the Aderet chose to finance the expenses of establishing and maintaining the eruv secretly from his own meager private funds, in order to prevent unnecessary disputes and to allow the residents of the city to carry on the Sabbath without concern.[1, 2]
The reform of measures and weights was a public-economic step with deep moral significance.[2] As part of his struggle against commercial corruption and with the aim of protecting the poorest consumers in the markets of Jerusalem, the Aderet ordered the replacement of the inaccurate wooden and stone weights that were common among the merchants with standard and accurate weights made of iron and copper.[2] This reform reflected his conception that the role of the rabbi is not confined to the doors of the study hall, but requires active involvement in repairing social and economic distortions in the free market.[2]
At the same time, the Aderet worked to strengthen the walls of kashrut and of the Sabbath in the city; he appointed new God-fearing ritual slaughterers, closely supervised the closing of the shops before the onset of the Sabbath and regulated the level of kashrut in the local bakeries.[2] Likewise, out of an understanding that there was a need for uniformity and halakhic clarity regarding the times of the day in the Land of Israel, he instructed the scholar and rabbi Yechiel Michel Tucazinsky to arrange and publish an updated and precise calendar of the times of the day according to the horizon of Jerusalem, which became a fundamental layer in the time-dependent laws throughout the Land of Israel.[2]
The Aderet invested enormous efforts in making peace and creating social solidarity among the various factions and communities in Jerusalem, and especially between the communities of the Hasidim and the Perushim (Mitnagdim), between whom a deep historical tension prevailed.[2] At the same time, he was required to answer intricate halakhic questions that came from the new agricultural colonies (moshavot) in the Land of Israel, and he dealt extensively with the commandments dependent on the Land from a statesmanlike and responsible view of the building of the Yishuv in the Land.[2] A deep and tragic spiritual aspect of his personality was his direct connection to the destruction of the Temple; his apartment in Jerusalem was located directly opposite the Temple Mount, and the Aderet said with pain that his living opposite the site of the Temple had shortened the years of his life, for every time he looked out of his window and saw the destruction of the Temple and the spiritual desolation prevailing there, he was seized with a deep anguish of the soul that irreversibly damaged his frail health.[1]
His Torah Teaching and Works: A Combination of Erudition, Analysis and Method
The Aderet was an extraordinarily prolific writer; he composed more than one hundred and twenty works covering all branches of the Torah: Scripture, halakha, Talmud, prayer, interpretation of Maimonides (Rambam), and spiritual autobiography.[2, 6] His Torah creativity is characterized by phenomenal erudition alongside sharpness and depth intended mainly for outstanding scholars.[4] His love for his manuscripts was enormous; he even discussed a principled and harrowing halakhic question: in the event of a fire in the house, must a person first save a kosher Torah scroll or rather his own handwritten Torah novellae, out of an understanding that the latter represent the unique spiritual toil of the learner, which may be lost forever.[4]
Among his personal works, "Seder Eliyahu" and "Nefesh David" stand out.[2, 7] The work "Seder Eliyahu" is a personal autobiographical diary written in the Aderet's own original handwriting in Jerusalem between the years 5662-5664 (1902-1904).[3] This unique work records his life story and his family history, and is filled with daily practices, personal stories and a constant striving for elevation of the soul and moral perfection.[3] The book was first printed in 5744, and another edition of it was published in 5770.[1] The printed edition of 5770 was partially censored; the editors omitted several passages that were not intended for a stranger's eye but only for the Aderet's descendants, and marked these omissions with three lines.[3] The original manuscript, consisting of 103 pages measuring 21x17 cm, contains the full text without these omissions.[3] The work has special ideological importance, since it continues the tradition of the practices and customs of the Vilna Gaon (the Gra).[3]
His additional book of memoirs and practices, "Nefesh David," which was published by Rabbi Moshe Zvi Neria, presents a deep moral and intellectual analysis of the human soul.[1, 2] The Aderet explains in this work that the spiritual structure of the human being is divided into three levels: nefesh, ruach and neshamah.[8] The lowest level is the "nefesh," in which dwell the impulses and the cravings for bodily and material matters, as one sees in the period of childhood and youth, which strives for the immediate satisfaction of desires.[8] The middle level is the "ruach," on which depend the feelings of honor, jealousy and pride, which are influenced by the vanities of this world, as it is said in Proverbs, "but a broken spirit (ruach) dries the bones."[8] Understanding this structure of the soul served the Aderet in formulating his moral guidance for his descendants.[2]
Another fascinating Torah work is "Shema Eliyahu," which is a Torah diary documenting halakhic deliberations with the great Torah sages whom the Aderet met in the course of his life.[2] Recently, photographs of his original manuscripts, among them the diary "Shema Eliyahu," reached the National Library.[9] On page 279 of the manuscript a fascinating historical passage was revealed that attests to the sharpness of the Torah debates in his generation; the Aderet there speaks sharply against an affront to the honor of the author of the "Chatam Sofer," and writes that the Gaon R. Yosef Rosen (the Rogatchover) of Dvinsk said that the words of the "Chatam Sofer" are "words of nonsense."[9] The disclosure of this passage, which in some of the printed editions was omitted and replaced with several dots in order to protect the honor of the rabbis, teaches about the high historical sensitivity and the scholarly tensions that prevailed among the giants of the generation.[9]
The Aderet's method of study combined phenomenal speed of comprehension with methodical depth and a complete aversion to the artificial and barren pilpul that was common in certain yeshivot in his generation.[4, 10] He strove to understand the fundamental principles of the Talmudic topic and of the halakhic ruling, with complete fidelity to the method of the Gra of Vilna, based on broad erudition and the comparison of sources.[3, 10] The Aderet's extraordinary humility prevented him from taking credit for himself; he used to honor every person, showed a generous eye and always sought out the spiritual virtues of those around him.[11]
The Encounter with Rav Kook and the Book "Eder HaYakar"
The close family bond between the Aderet and his son-in-law, Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaKohen Kook, became one of the most significant spiritual encounters in the history of Jewish thought in the modern era.[1, 2, 12] Rav Kook saw his father-in-law as an exemplary figure embodying the religious perfection that seeks to connect "the spiritual Torah" (the world of faith, Kabbalah and thought) with "the practical Torah" (the world of halakha, its rules and practical details).[13] In Rav Kook's view, these two Torahs were completely united in the period of the prophets and the Tannaim, and the course of the Jerusalem Talmud reflects this harmonious union.[13] The figure of the Aderet, who lived entirely within the world of practical halakha and yet was imbued with a natural love of God, fear of Heaven and profound humility, symbolized for Rav Kook the real possibility of reviving this union in the present generation.[11]
Toward the end of the year of mourning for the Aderet, at the beginning of the year 5666 (1906), Rav Kook published the monumental work "Eder HaYakar" in memory of his father-in-law.[12, 14, 15] The name of the book is derived from the initials of the name of the deceased – Eliyahu David Rabinowitz – and its source is in the verse from the book of Zechariah: "Cast it to the potter, the goodly price (eder ha-yakar) at which I was valued by them."[14] Although the book extensively sketches the features of the Aderet's character and incorporates autobiographical passages from his writings, most of it is devoted to the clarification of deep intellectual, faith-related and theological questions of its author.[12, 14] Rav Kook used the figure and practices of his father-in-law as a basis for developing his original teaching on faith, as detailed in the structure of the book's chapters.[12]
Although the book deals mainly with matters of faith and thought, Rav Kook incorporates in it several principled halakhic discussions.[12] A particularly prominent discussion concerns the source of the obligation to observe customs in Israel.[12] Although the Talmud in Tractate Pesachim relies on the verse "Hear, my son, the instruction of your father, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother" as the source of the obligation to observe customs, Rav Kook presents a position according to which there is no formal obligation whatsoever from the Torah, from the Prophets or from the words of the Sages to observe these customs.[12] In his view, the true and deep source of the validity of custom stems from the shared "love of the nation" and from the vital need of Knesset Israel (the Congregation of Israel) to preserve its identity and solidarity throughout the generations.[12]
In 5727 (1967) the son of Rav Kook, Rabbi Zvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook (the Ratzyah), published a new edition of the book "Eder HaYakar" in one volume together with the work "Ikvei HaTzon" (which includes the well-known essays "Ma'amar HaDor," "HaPachad" and "HaOneg VeHaSimchah").[12, 14] To this edition the Ratzyah appended twenty valuable halakhic and personal letters written by the Aderet, which illuminate the depth of his ties with the great figures of his generation.[12] A further edition of the book, which includes a detailed commentary by Rabbi Shlomo Aviner, was published in the year 5773 (2013), a fact attesting to the continuing vitality of the teaching and memory of the Aderet among students of Torah and of Jewish thought in the Land of Israel.[14]

title: The Work and Torah Teaching of the Aderet – Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim
source_file: פועלו ומשנתו התורנית של האדרת – רבי אליהו דוד רבינוביץ-תאומים.docx
content:
The Work and Torah Teaching of the Aderet – Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim
Introduction: The Spiritual and Historical Portrait of the Gaon, the Aderet
Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim (the Aderet; 5603–5665, 1843–1905) is counted among the most complex, impressive and influential Torah figures to emerge from the Lithuanian Torah world in the second half of the 19th century, and in the leadership of the Old Yishuv in Jerusalem at the beginning of the 20th century [cite: 1, 2]. His spiritual figure embodied a rare fusion of scholarly genius and phenomenal mastery of every branch of Torah, together with inner piety, asceticism, extreme humility and deep moral and social sensitivity [cite: 1, 3, 4]. The Aderet left behind a Torah legacy of vast scope, numbering more than one hundred and twenty works in manuscript, dealing with Scripture, the Mishnah, the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds, halakha, thought and mussar [cite: 2, 4].
The stations of his life – from his childhood in Pikeln, through the major rabbinic posts in the towns of Ponevezh and Mir, to his immigration to the Land of Israel as deputy and designated successor of the rabbi of Jerusalem, Rabbi Shmuel Salant – reflect the vicissitudes of the period in the Jewish world [cite: 2, 3, 5]. His close family ties with his son-in-law, our master Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaKohen Kook, added a highly significant historical and ideological dimension to his legacy, as the figure of the Aderet served as a connecting link between the classical Lithuanian Torah world and the movement of spiritual and national revival in the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 3, 6, 7].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life and the Stages of His Rabbinic Leadership
Early Years, Orphanhood and Torah Upbringing
Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim was born on the festival of Shavuot 5603 (June 4, 1843) in the town of Pikeln in Lithuania (then within the Pale of Settlement of the Russian Empire), together with his twin brother Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda [cite: 2]. The two were born to their father Rabbi Binyamin Rabinowitz, one of the great Torah scholars of his generation and of an illustrious lineage traced to the author of the "Levushim" and to the Chacham Tzvi, and to their mother Toiba [cite: 2, 4]. When he was only five years old his mother died, and his father was forced to bear alone the burden of raising the twins under conditions of extremely harsh poverty and want [cite: 2, 4]. When he was nine the family moved to the town of Shilel, where the father was appointed rabbi of the community [cite: 2].
A fierce soul-love prevailed between the Aderet and his twin brother Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda, which the Aderet described in his personal diary in the words: "I loved him with an everlasting love, truly as my own soul" [cite: 2]. While still in their youth, between the ages of thirteen and fifteen, the twins jointly composed comprehensive scholarly works: "Shevet Achim" (Brothers Dwelling Together) on the rules of the Talmud, and "Bnei Binyamin" (Sons of Binyamin) on Maimonides' Mishneh Torah [cite: 2, 8]. In 5620 (1860), when he was about sixteen, the family moved to the town of Ariogala (Ragali), where the Aderet began writing his comprehensive work on Maimonides, "Ma'asei La-Melekh" (Deeds for the King) [cite: 2, 4]. That same year he married Feiga Mina, daughter of R. Aryeh Leib Chazan of Ponevezh, and moved to devote himself to his Torah study in the kloyz in Ponevezh, where he testified of himself that he reviewed the entire Talmud rapidly and that his memory absorbed all of the learning [cite: 2].
The Rabbinate of Ponevezh (5632–5653)
In 5632 (1872), at only twenty-nine years of age, the Aderet was appointed rabbi of the city of Ponevezh – one of the most important and central communities of Lithuania – after the departure of Rabbi Hillel Milikowsky [cite: 2, 3]. The Aderet held this position for eighteen years, during which his moral and halakhic leadership stood out [cite: 2, 3]. He devoted his time and energy to caring for the city's poor, orphans and widows, and even took upon himself personal financial debts in order to support the needy [cite: 2]. Because of these debts he was prevented from accepting the prestigious offer of the rabbinate of the city of Warsaw, since he refused to leave Ponevezh before repaying his debts to the lenders from whom he had borrowed for the benefit of the city's poor [cite: 2].
The years of his tenure in Ponevezh were steeped in personal grief and family tragedies. His salary was extremely meager, and his family suffered abject poverty. Of the twelve children born to him, seven died young from illnesses and from lack of medical means [cite: 2, 3]. Despite the heavy mourning and the economic distress, the Aderet refused to lord it over the members of his community, and expressed in his writings a deep aversion to the trappings of pride and rabbinic authority [cite: 3]. When the rabbinate of the city of Vilkomir was offered to him in 5643, he agreed to remain in Ponevezh at the request of the community members, who promised to raise his salary, although in practice he continued to suffer severe economic hardship [cite: 2].
The Leadership of the Mir Community (5653–5661)
In 5653 (1893), after yielding to the repeated entreaties of the leaders of the town of Mir, the Aderet left Ponevezh and moved to serve as rabbi and av beit din (head of the rabbinic court) of Mir [cite: 2, 3, 7, 9]. The departure involved great tension, as the residents of Ponevezh tried to prevent his leaving and even forbade the wagon drivers to carry his books out of the city [cite: 4, 10].
The Aderet served in Mir for eight years (5653–5661, 1893–1901) [cite: 7, 9]. His tenure in this town was interwoven with a close bond with the famous Mir Yeshiva [cite: 3, 7, 11]. The Aderet worked for the spiritual flourishing of the yeshiva and drew its students close. Testimony to the enormous esteem in which the sages of the generation held him was given when the Gaon Rabbi Eliyahu Baruch Kamai came to serve alongside him in Mir, and the Aderet recited over him, with the Divine Name and Kingship, the blessing "who has apportioned of His wisdom to those who fear Him" [cite: 11].
Immigration to the Land of Israel and the Leadership of the Jerusalem Community (5661–5665)
The Aderet's deep aspiration to immigrate to the Land of Israel accompanied him from his youth, but a lack of financial means delayed its fulfillment [cite: 3]. The turning point came in 5659 (1899), when Rabbi Shmuel Salant, the aged rabbi of the Ashkenazi community in Jerusalem, whose eyesight had greatly weakened, asked the city's sages to find an outstanding rabbi to serve as his assistant and future successor [cite: 2, 3, 5]. On the warm recommendation of the leader of the great sages of Lithuania, Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski of Vilna, the offer was directed to the Aderet [cite: 3].
In the month of Adar 5661 (1901) the Aderet arrived in Jerusalem and was received with great honor as leader and rabbi alongside Rabbi Shmuel Salant [cite: 2, 3, 5, 8]. His leadership in Jerusalem was characterized by full harmony with Rabbi Shmuel Salant and by vigorous public activity to improve halakhic and social norms [cite: 8, 12]. Among his notable actions was the establishment of a comprehensive eruv system connecting the Old City with the new neighborhoods outside the walls, a project that the Aderet financed largely from his own pocket in secret [cite: 2, 4, 8].
His days in Jerusalem were short. The Aderet experienced deep and constant grief at the sight of the destruction of the Temple, and even remarked that his dwelling place, which looked directly out onto the Temple Mount, shortened his days from excess of sorrow [cite: 2, 4]. On 3 Adar I 5665 (February 8, 1905), at only 61 years of age, the Aderet passed away while Rabbi Shmuel Salant was still alive [cite: 2, 5]. In his last moments he read the passages of the tefillin and passed away, and he was buried in the cemetery on the Mount of Olives [cite: 2].

Literary Creativity and the Torah Enterprise
The Aderet was one of the most prolific authors of recent generations, and committed to writing some 120 works in every field of Torah [cite: 1, 4]. This writing enterprise stemmed from an unceasing inner drive to study and to innovate, with every available moment devoted to putting his thoughts in writing [cite: 4]. Although some of his writings were burned in fires that broke out in his home and most were not printed in his lifetime, in recent decades Torah institutes (among them Machon Yerushalayim and Machon Ahavat Shalom) have been diligently publishing his writings [cite: 2, 4, 14].
Cheshbonot shel Mitzvah
The work "Cheshbonot shel Mitzvah" (Reckonings of the Commandment) is considered one of the Aderet's central and most profound Torah enterprises [cite: 14, 15]. The work is built as a series of novellae, notes and comprehensive scholarly discussions on "Sefer ha-Chinukh" (The Book of Education), and to a large extent presents a rich scholarly alternative to the book "Minchat Chinukh" [cite: 14, 15]. In this work the Aderet analyzes the 613 commandments, their definitions and their halakhic ramifications, with complete command of the Bavli, the Yerushalmi, the Rishonim and the Acharonim [cite: 14, 15]. The book was published from the author's manuscript with the addition of comprehensive references and sources [cite: 14].
Seder Eliyahu and Nefesh David
This pair of works constitutes a rare historical, moral and spiritual asset in rabbinic literature:
Seder Eliyahu (The Order of Eliyahu): a personal autobiographical work written by the Aderet, detailing the events of his life from the day of his birth until his immigration to Jerusalem [cite: 2, 16, 17]. Keeping the diary served him as a refuge for his soul in turbulent periods [cite: 17]. The work includes detailed historical documentation of the communities in which he served, a rare candor regarding his dilemmas and sufferings, and a profound description of his inner service of God [cite: 4, 16, 17].
Nefesh David (The Soul of David): a booklet of practices, mussar and a spiritual testament intended for his sons [cite: 2, 3, 16, 17]. In this work the Aderet details his ways of life, his personal customs and his guidance in the service of God – such as extreme caution against pride, love of the commandments (such as joy in the commandment of the sukkah), and complete distancing from the pursuit of honor and authority [cite: 3, 4, 18].
Tefillah le-David and Over Orach
Tefillah le-David (A Prayer of David): a comprehensive work devoted entirely to matters of prayer, its versions, its intentions and its halakhic laws [cite: 19, 20, 21]. The work includes profound studies of the prayer book, glosses on the Shulchan Arukh, and discussions of kabbalistic and halakhic topics (such as the obligation of the Levites to wash the hands of the Kohanim) [cite: 21, 22].
Over Orach (Wayfarer): novellae, glosses and halakhic notes that the Aderet recorded following the order of Shulchan Arukh Orach Chaim, dealing with daily laws, prayer customs and the festivals [cite: 4, 23].
Other Notable Works
Ma'asei La-Melekh: comprehensive novellae and explanations on Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, written in two thick notebooks beginning at age 16 [cite: 2, 4].
Bnei Binyamin: notes and discussions on Maimonides, composed in partnership with his twin brother Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda [cite: 2].
Ohalei David (Tents of David): a collection of halakhic questions and responsa sent to him from all over the Jewish diaspora [cite: 4, 10].
Kava de-Kashyata (A Measure of Difficulties): a compilation of severe difficulties from the writings of his father, Rabbi Binyamin [cite: 4].
Seder Mo'adot (The Order of the Festivals), Sod Yere'im (on Sefer Yere'im), Ateret Adar (on the Ba'al ha-Turim), and Seder Parshiyot (on the Torah) [cite: 2, 4].

His Halakhic Teaching: Methodology, Leadership and the Commandments Dependent on the Land
Halakhic Methodology and Precision in the Commandments
The halakhic teaching of the Aderet was founded on a fusion of profound textual mastery of all the foundational books with complete fidelity to the tradition of halakhic ruling [cite: 1, 4, 10]. His halakhic outlook was characterized by meticulous precision in the details of the laws, out of a deep fear of transgressing the words of the Sages [cite: 4]. The Aderet used to go about throughout the hours of the day adorned with small tefillin, and was careful to recite the Shema ke-vatikin (in the manner of the scrupulous) before sunrise, even in the Lithuanian summer days when sunrise falls at an extremely early hour [cite: 2, 8].
On the other hand, his rulings were not detached from the needs of reality. The Aderet displayed great social and human sensitivity. For example, in a halakhic discussion concerning permission for construction by non-Jewish workers on the Sabbath under contract for Jews (in order to prevent heavy financial loss caused by the authorities' laws of rest on Sundays), he tended to examine grounds for leniency out of an understanding of the difficult situation of those choosing to build their homes in the Land of Israel [cite: 10].
His Attitude to Customs and Public Enactments
The Aderet displayed a complex position toward public customs. On the one hand, he expressed deep sorrow over customs that had taken root among the people and contradicted settled halakhot – such as the improper multiplication of aliyot on Simchat Torah, the abolition of the priestly blessing (nesiat kapayim) because of the drinking of wines, or the abolition of the recitation of "Ein Ke-Eloheinu" after the Musaf prayer [cite: 10]. On the other hand, he showed humility and extreme caution about actually making changes in public synagogues [cite: 10]. In his diary he testified that in the public synagogue he left the customs as they had been, out of respect for the Geonim who preceded him, whereas the changes and corrections he made according to the strict law were applied only in the small minyan conducted in his private home [cite: 10].
The Commandments Dependent on the Land and His Work in Jerusalem
Upon his immigration to Jerusalem, the Aderet placed the topic of the commandments dependent on the Land at the center of his halakhic concerns [cite: 10, 13]. He was pained by the stumbling block of eating untithed produce (tevel) at the time of the grape harvest and the reaping of grain, and turned to his son-in-law, Rav Kook, with a request to compose a short and clear guide in the vernacular (Yiddish) to the laws of separating terumot and ma'asrot [cite: 13]. Moreover, the Aderet conceived an original idea: to conclude a public and solemn "covenant of commitment" of the entire Yishuv in the Land of Israel to observe the commandments dependent on the Land and on the Temple, after the model of the covenant concluded by the returnees from the Babylonian exile in the days of Nehemiah [cite: 10].
On the practical level in Jerusalem, his enterprise of repairing the city's eruv stood out. Until his arrival, the topographic and halakhic complexity of Jerusalem outside the walls created difficulties for carrying on the Sabbath [cite: 2, 4]. The Aderet initiated, planned and established a comprehensive eruv system connecting the Old City with the new neighborhoods, while bearing the financial expenses of the project in secret from his meager pocket [cite: 2, 4, 8].

The Complex and Deep Relationship with His Son-in-Law, the Raayah Kook
The Family and Personal Relationship
In 5646 (1886) the Aderet married off his eldest daughter, Altah Bat-Sheva, to the young prodigy Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaKohen Kook (the Raayah) [cite: 2, 12]. The marriage laid the foundation for an exceptionally deep spiritual and emotional bond between father-in-law and son-in-law [cite: 2, 12]. However, only three years later (5649, 1889), Altah Bat-Sheva died in the prime of her life, leaving behind an infant daughter (Freida Chana) [cite: 2, 3, 12].
The Aderet, who was bound by cords of love to the Raayah and feared the severing of the family tie with him, turned to Rav Kook and proposed that he marry his niece – Reiza Rivka, daughter of his twin brother Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda [cite: 2, 3]. Rav Kook accepted the proposal, and from this match was born his only son, Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook [cite: 3]. The bond between the two continued to deepen, and the Aderet urged Rav Kook to immigrate to the Land of Israel, at the time when the Aderet was serving in Jerusalem and the Raayah was invited to serve as rabbi of Jaffa and the moshavot [cite: 12].
Mutual Esteem and Spiritual Influence
The Aderet held his son-in-law the Raayah in enormous esteem. When the people of Ponevezh marveled at Rav Kook's Torah genius, the Aderet said to them: "Indeed you have already managed to perceive that he is great in Torah, but you do not yet know how great he is in the fear of God" [cite: 3]. On another occasion he remarked with humility: "I have taken a son-in-law whose ankles I do not reach" [cite: 3]. The Aderet's son, Rabbi Avraham Moshe, later served as the personal secretary of the Raayah Kook in Jerusalem [cite: 4].
The Book "Eder ha-Yakar"
A short time after the passing of the Aderet in 5665, the Raayah Kook composed his famous book "Eder ha-Yakar" (The Precious Mantle) (published in Jaffa in 5666-1906) [cite: 2, 6]. The title of the book derives from the prophecy of Zechariah (11:13) and forms an acronym: Eliyahu David Rabinowitz ha-Yakar (the precious) [cite: 6, 24].
The book is not merely a biography; Rav Kook wove into it features of the spiritual and moral figure of his father-in-law, incorporating autobiographical passages from the writings of the Aderet [cite: 6, 25]. Alongside the portrayal of the figure, the Raayah used the work to present his profound philosophical and intellectual teaching on the generation of revival, the redemption of Israel, and the need for a connection between the spiritual strength of the old generation and the national commitment of the young generation [cite: 6, 26].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Influence, Legacy and Imprint for Generations
The legacy of Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim, the Aderet, has remained one of the most glorious exemplars of Torah leadership in recent generations [cite: 1, 3]. His figure represents a rare synthesis of:
Toil in Torah and literary prolificacy: the writing of dozens of works in every field of Torah, combining phenomenal mastery and depth of analysis [cite: 1, 4].
Piety, mussar and humility: flight from authority, extreme caution against pride, and an exceptional love of the commandments that does not depend on any reward [cite: 3, 4].
Public self-sacrifice: bearing the burden of the people, repaying the debts of the poor from his own pocket, and correcting public arrangements such as the Jerusalem eruv and the regulation of the commandments dependent on the Land [cite: 2, 4, 8, 13].
A bridge between worlds: a deep bond with the Lithuanian yeshiva world, leadership in old Jerusalem, and a formative influence on the worldview of his son-in-law the Raayah Kook and on Religious Zionism on the one hand, alongside enormous esteem in the Haredi world on the other [cite: 1, 3, 6, 7].
His works being published in our generation are enjoying a renewed flowering, and his figure continues to serve as a source of inspiration for toil in Torah, for moral integrity and for the service of God out of love and holy humility.
